issues.legal_issue: A later suit for specific performance is not barred for omitting that relief from an earlier suit for permanent injunction when the two claims arise from independent causes of action.
material_facts: The plaintiff first sued for permanent injunction after the defendant allegedly threatened to dispossess him from premises he occupied under an agreement to sell.
The later suit sought specific performance of the agreement to sell.

The causes of action differed: the injunction claim arose from the alleged threat to possession, while the specific-performance claim arose from the date fixed for performance or the defendant's refusal to perform.
The factual ingredients and limitation periods for the two claims were different.
issues.conclusion: The specific-performance suit was not barred by Order 2 Rule 2 and was maintainable for trial on the merits; the courts below erred in rejecting the plaint on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Order 2 Rule 2(1) requires a plaintiff to include the whole claim arising from the cause of action pleaded, and Rule 2(2) bars a later suit for relief omitted from the earlier suit only when that relief was available on the earlier suit's cause of action. A claim for injunction based on threatened interference with possession has a distinct cause of action from a claim for specific performance, which arises on the date fixed for performance or on refusal when no date is fixed. The Court relied on Order 39 Rule 1(c), Articles 85, 86 and 87 and Article 54 of the Limitation Act, and Rathnavathi v. Kavita Ganashamdas (2015) 5 SCC 223.

rule.if: followup_specific_performance_suit and earlier_injunction_suit and claims_have_independent_causes and different_factual_ingredients and separate_limitation_triggers

predicates.followup_specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brings a later suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell after an earlier suit concerning the same property.
predicates.earlier_injunction_suit: The plaintiff's earlier suit sought protection against threatened interference with the plaintiff's possession.
predicates.claims_have_independent_causes: The earlier claim arose from threatened interference with possession, while the later claim arose from the date for contractual performance or the defendant's refusal to perform.
predicates.different_factual_ingredients: The facts needed to establish the possession-protection claim differed from those needed to establish the contract-enforcement claim.
predicates.separate_limitation_triggers: The periods for bringing the two claims began from different events.

issues.definition: When a later contract-enforcement suit follows an earlier possession-protection suit and the claims rest on independent causes with different facts and limitation triggers, the later suit is not barred by omission of that relief from the earlier suit.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff may bring a fresh suit after withdrawing an earlier suit when the plaintiff stated an intention to pursue fresh proceedings and the court permitted withdrawal, even if the withdrawal order did not expressly grant liberty to file a fresh suit.
material_facts: In the earlier permanent-injunction suit, the plaintiff told the court that he wished to withdraw the suit to pursue appropriate proceedings before the competent forum.
The court recorded that statement and allowed the plaintiff to withdraw the suit.
The withdrawal order did not separately state that the plaintiff had liberty to file a fresh suit.
The plaintiff later filed a suit for specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The recorded statement read together with the court's permission to withdraw satisfied the requirement for pursuing a fresh suit, and the omission of express liberty in the order did not prevent the suit from proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 23 Rule 1(3), the court may permit withdrawal in circumstances allowing a fresh suit. The order must be read together with the plaintiff's recorded statement; the statement may form part of the order granting permission. Applying Gurinderpal v. Jagmittar Singh (2004) 11 SCC 219, the Court held that an order need not separately recite liberty to file afresh when the recorded statement and order together show that the suit was withdrawn so the plaintiff could pursue a fresh proceeding. The Court also noted that the bar under Order 2 Rule 2 must be strictly construed.

predicates.fresh_suit_after_withdrawal: A plaintiff brings a new suit after withdrawing an earlier suit.
predicates.plaintiff_stated_intent_to_pursue_fresh_: The plaintiff told the court when seeking withdrawal that the plaintiff intended to pursue appropriate fresh proceedings.
predicates.court_allowed_withdrawal: The court recorded the plaintiff's statement and permitted withdrawal of the earlier suit.
predicates.order_omitted_explicit_refiling_permissi: The withdrawal order did not separately state that a fresh suit could be filed.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff states an intention to pursue fresh proceedings and the court permits withdrawal, the fresh suit may proceed even if the order does not expressly grant permission to refile.
